text.description:
The Pedro de Osma Museum is a museum in Barranco. It is a good first stop on this map because you can photograph the building from a short, easy distance without needing to go inside. You can frame the whole frontage with very little walking, and there is room to step a little left or right to change the angle.

The building works well as a subject because its entrance, walls and any garden greenery give clear shapes, textures and colour. These show up well on a phone screen. Start with a wide, straight-on shot to record the whole building, then move closer for details such as the doorway, windows or decorative features. Details make a good second picture and help your set of photos feel varied.

Keep the phone level, using the gridlines so that vertical lines stay straight. If people walk through the scene, wait a moment for a gap, or include one person to give a sense of scale. Check the official site before you go if you also want to visit the inside, as access to museums can be ticketed or restricted.
text.geographic_location: The Pedro de Osma Museum is in the Barranco district.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so use the map to navigate to the Pedro de Osma Museum. From it the museum is about 19 metres to the north-east, less than a minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole frontage in, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. The building will be in front of you with room to spare, so you can step sideways to find the angle you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of the entrance or a detail. Keep the phone upright to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so that the walls keep their colour. Use portrait mode only if you want a person in front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls, and it is often quieter.

text.access_note: The building can be photographed from outside, but access to the museum itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bridge of Sighs
label: Bridge of Sighs
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1550043240: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puente de Los Suspiros' (30 m across).
notes: Wooden footbridge and symbol of bohemian Barranco.

text.description: The Bridge of Sighs (Puente de los Suspiros) is a wooden footbridge in the middle of old Barranco, and one of the most visited spots in the district. It is 44 metres long and 3 metres wide, and it links Ayacucho Street with the Paseo Chabuca Granda, the walkway that leads up towards the Hermitage of Barranco. Underneath, the road down to the beaches (the Bajada de Baños) runs through the ravine, so the bridge sits eight and a half metres or so above it. It photographs well because it is a simple shape: a long, slim wooden span with railings that draw the eye along it, set among the old streets and buildings. Local tradition made it a meeting place for couples, which is how it got its name. It opened on 14 February 1876 and was destroyed during the War of the Pacific in 1881. In 1960 the composer Chabuca Granda dedicated a waltz to it, and a monument to her stands nearby. The bridge was restored and reopened in December 2014. In June 2023 part of a neighbouring old building partly collapsed, the area including the bridge was closed, and reconstruction was announced. Access may therefore have changed, so check the official site before you go. If it is open, try the default lens first and switch to ultra-wide if the whole bridge does not fit. Wait a moment for people to move out of the shot, or include one or two to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Barranco district, Lima, between the Hermitage of Barranco and the Paseo Chabuca Granda, spanning the ravine road that runs down to the beaches.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops to give you a starting point, so go to central Barranco first and then walk to the Paseo Chabuca Granda, next to the Hermitage of Barranco. The bridge is about 35 m to the east of it, so walk east to reach it. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole bridge does not fit, or if people or railings crowd the edges. Use telephoto (2x or more) for close shots of the wooden railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the deck up with a horizontal line so the bridge looks level. Let the railings lead the eye along the bridge, and keep a little space on both sides. Hold the phone at chest height for a natural view, or crouch slightly to make the bridge look longer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. Take a few frames in a row, as people walk across all the time. A Live Photo can help you pick a moment with a clear deck.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In the afternoon the sun is behind you and lights the front of the bridge. In the morning you are looking towards the sun, so the bridge may look dark and you should lower the exposure a little.

text.access_note: The bridge was closed to the public in 2023 after damage to a neighbouring building and reconstruction was announced, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, looking east, the morning sun is in front of you and the afternoon sun is behind you.
The bridge is usually busy with visitors, so people are likely to appear in the frame.
The railings of a wooden bridge create leading lines that work well in a photo.

name: Bajada de Baños
label: Bajada de Baños
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puente de los Suspiros' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Puente de Los Suspiros' (way/1550043240): middle (30 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W159608949 (Bajada de Baños): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Picturesque stone-paved path descending from the bridge to the sea.

text.description:
Bajada de Baños is a stepped pedestrian path that drops from the edge of Barranco down a ravine toward the sea. Its walls are covered in colourful murals, which makes it a good place for a phone camera: there is colour everywhere, and the steps give the picture a strong line that leads the eye downhill.

The recommended vantage point is the upper, Barranco-side end of the wooden footbridge, the Puente de los Suspiros. The raised deck looks down the ravine, so you get the mural-lined steps falling away toward the sea with part of the bridge in the frame.

The Bajada is a narrow path rather than a wide square, so there is no single big viewpoint. Every angle gives a different picture, and it is worth walking a little way down to shoot the murals, steps and path from within. Take a few frames from the bridge first, then go down for close-ups.

If you want a wider view out to sea, there is a lookout beside the bridge that looks over the coast, with the bridge and the top of the Bajada at the edge of the frame.

The stairs are steep in places, so allow time and energy for the walk back up. The lower section near the coast is fenced and roofed, which may limit open-air views down there.
text.geographic_location: Bajada de Baños is in Barranco. It runs down the ravine from beside the Puente de los Suspiros toward the coast.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot; head for the Puente de los Suspiros in Barranco. Once you arrive, the upper, Barranco-side end of the bridge is the recommended vantage point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the bridge, the steps and the murals into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the path, and 2x if your phone has it to pick out a single mural or a section of steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Puente de los Suspiros (upper (Barranco-side) end, looking down the Bajada). The stepped, mural-lined Bajada falling away below the wooden footbridge toward the sea, with the bridge itself in the frame. Then walk a little way down the steps for views from within the Bajada.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the line of the steps as a leading line, with the bridge at one side. Keep the phone level so the steps do not lean. For a different picture, go down onto the Bajada and shoot along the path with murals on both sides. For a seaward view, try the lookout next to the bridge, with the bridge and the top of the Bajada at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mid-tone of the steps to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Wait a moment for people to clear the steps, or use a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and fewer people on the narrow steps, but check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The Bajada is a pedestrian stepped path with steep sections; check local information before you go.

name: Parque Municipal de Barranco
label: Main Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Municipal de Barranco' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque Municipal de Barranco' (way/436583900): middle (136 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W603127555 (Parque Municipal de Barranco): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Central plaza with the municipal hall and colourful surroundings.

text.description:
Parque Municipal de Barranco is a public park in Barranco with lawns, trees and a few good small subjects close together. Around the central fountain and the pergola stage you get marble statues, cherub figures and the naiads' fountain, all set against the historic buildings around the park. These include the Iglesia Santísima Cruz and the municipal library. That mix of garden detail and old façades is why it works so well on a phone. You can shoot a close subject with a pleasant background without moving more than a few steps.

Start at the fountain and pergola stage. Take one wide frame to show the whole scene, then move in on the statues and the Candelabro Barberini. The statues facing the church make a good pairing: put a statue in the foreground and let the church sit behind it. For a different view, walk to Avenida Pedro de Osma, the street that leads into the park. From there you can catch the lawns, the pond and the tree-lined walkways. If you also want a wider view of the neighbourhood and the ocean beyond, the Puente de los Suspiros offers one.

Take a few extra frames of each subject, because people walking through can spoil a single shot. Sunset and early morning are the best times, when soft light brings out the carving and the architecture.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Barranco, the seaside district of Lima, in the municipal park surrounded by the Iglesia Santísima Cruz and the municipal library.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops to give you here; head to central Barranco and look for Parque Municipal de Barranco. The park's centre, with the fountain and pergola stage, is about 56 m to the north-west, roughly a minute's walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the buildings behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the stage, fountain and church in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statue and cherub details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Municipal de Barranco (inside the park, around the central fountain and the pergola stage). The park's central fountain, marble statues and stage framed by the surrounding historic buildings, including the Iglesia Santísima Cruz and the municipal library.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the fountain or a statue on one of the lines, with the church or library filling the background. Keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight by holding the phone level. For a wider alternative, try the lawns and pond from Avenida Pedro de Osma, or the view over the neighbourhood from the Puente de los Suspiros.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue or fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white marble and bright sky do not wash out. Use portrait mode on a single statue, but check that the edges of the stone are still cleanly outlined.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or early morning, when the soft light brings out the architectural details.

text.access_note: This looks like an open public park, but check the official site before you go for any opening times or restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: The park is a public, open green space in central Barranco, Lima.
Passers-by may walk through the frame, so taking several shots of the same subject helps.
Marble can look overexposed in bright light, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
The park may be quiet on weekday mornings.

label: MAC Lima
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: Contemporary art museum in Barranco's park.

text.description:
The Museum of Contemporary Art of Lima, known as MAC Lima, is the city's contemporary art museum, set in the Barranco district. It was designed by the Peruvian architect Frederick Cooper Llosa and built on land given by the Municipality of Barranco. It runs as a private non-profit organisation. The museum opened formally in late January 2013, on ground once occupied by the Barranco Zoo and its artificial lake. The zoo closed in 1970, and the building now stands on top of the old lake. The museum itself grew out of an Institute of Contemporary Art that began in 1955 and moved between several buildings before this one.

For a phone photo, the appeal is a large, modern building. The outline is about 187 m across, so the main challenge is fitting enough of it into the frame. Start with a wide shot to show the whole building, then move closer for details such as edges, entrances, signs and any people passing by. In December 2024 the museum opened Contemporáneo 1, an exhibition of its permanent collection, so there may be art worth a picture inside. Check the official site for visiting details and photography rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Barranco district of Lima, on the site of the former Barranco Zoo and its artificial lake. The land was donated by the Municipality of Barranco.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head to the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo (MAC Lima). The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole building, because it is very wide. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of one section. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as entrances, signs or surface textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Use it as a starting point. For a wide shot, move back as far as the surroundings allow, or look for a spot with a clear view, until the full width fits. Then walk closer for detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with the grid so it looks straight. Keep the phone level, because tilting it makes large buildings lean. Try one wide frame with some sky and one tighter frame on a single feature, and wait for a person to walk through to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Take a quick panorama only if the building is too wide for the ultra-wide, and hold the phone steady while you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the building.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening arrangements, entry rules and whether photography is allowed inside the exhibition rooms.

name: Hermitage of Barranco
label: Ermita de Barranco
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plazuela Chabuca Granda' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plazuela Chabuca Granda' (way/522161923): middle (15 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/389383049: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia La Ermita de Barranco' (62 m across).
notes: Small white church at the head of the Bridge of Sighs.

text.description:
The Hermitage of Barranco, the Ermita, is a small Catholic church that stands beside the Bridge of Sighs in the district's historic centre. It began in the mid-18th century as a modest chapel for fishermen and travellers. Local legend says the spot is where the district began, after two lost fishermen were guided ashore by the light of a cross. The church was burned in 1881 during the War of the Pacific and rebuilt the following year. It has been closed since the 1974 earthquake, and its roof has largely collapsed, so what you photograph is the outside: a pink-and-yellow adobe facade and a roofless shell.

That weathered shell is what makes it work as a picture. Seen from the small plaza in front, the facade stands against the edge of the coastal cliff, with the ocean beyond. The plaza is named after the singer Chabuca Granda, and it was opened in 1992. Guides often recommend it at sunset, and it is the usual place for the classic front view.

Stand in the plaza beside the entrance steps and keep the whole building in the frame. Then take a second, closer shot of the textured walls. The path called Bajada de los Baños gives a different view with the church perched above the cobbled walkway. It is steep and can be busy, so keep your phone close and watch your footing. Between roughly May and October the coastal mist can flatten the sky, so a clear evening gives the best colour.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Barranco, Lima, beside the Bridge of Sighs, next to the Plazuela Chabuca Granda, at the edge of the coastal cliff.
text.directions_text: Head for Barranco's historic centre and the Bridge of Sighs on foot or by any local transport, as there is no station or tram stop right at this spot. The church stands right beside the bridge, with the Plazuela Chabuca Granda in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full facade with the cliff edge and ocean behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the plaza and entrance steps in the frame too, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the weathered walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plazuela Chabuca Granda (in front of the church, beside the entrance steps). The pink-and-yellow adobe facade and roofless shell of the church, framed against the coastal cliff edge and the ocean beyond. The church lies to the south-west of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the walls stand straight. Leave some sky and sea above and behind the building to show how it sits on the cliff. For a different shot, go down to the Bajada de los Baños and photograph the church perched above the cobbled path, with the walkway and street art in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour and the walls do not wash out. Try a Live Photo if people are passing in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset on clear days. Between roughly May and October the coastal mist can flatten the sky.

text.access_note: The plaza is a free public space, but the church itself has been closed to the public since 1974, so photograph the outside only; check local news for any works or changes before you go.

text.description: The Iglesia de la Santísima Cruz stands directly in front of Barranco's central park. The park gives you open ground to step back on, and you can see the whole front of the building. The most rewarding view is the frontal facade with the bell tower, framed by the trees of the park. The foliage adds a natural border to the picture. A good photo here is mostly about distance. Walk out into the park, turn round, and let the church fill the middle of the frame with a little greenery around it. Take a few versions: one wide, with the trees and some of the park in the foreground, and one tighter, aimed at the tower and the upper part of the front. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. The gridlines help with this. If people wander into the shot, wait a moment, as the park is a public space and the crowd keeps moving. The church is also a working place of worship, so keep a respectful distance from anyone going in, and if you plan to go inside, check current opening hours and any festival-related street closures before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Barranco, on the side of the Parque Municipal de Barranco, the district's central park, with the church facing the park.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Barranco and the Parque Municipal de Barranco. From there the church is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and bell tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of trees and park in the shot, and keep the church away from the edges of the frame so it does not stretch. Use 2x-3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pick out the bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Municipal de Barranco (across the park, facing the church front). The church's frontal facade and bell tower, framed by the trees of the central park.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the church in the middle third, with the tower upright and level. Let branches or treetops make a loose frame at the top or the sides. For a second shot, zoom in on the bell tower and the upper facade. Take a portrait of your group with the church behind them, using portrait mode only if the church still looks sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade does not wash out. Do not use portrait mode for the whole-church picture, as it can blur the edges of the building. Take a Live Photo as well if people are passing through the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not directly behind the church, and the facade is evenly lit. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, and fewer people in the park.

text.access_note: The park in front is an open public space; the church is a place of worship, so check current opening hours and any festival-related street closures before you go if you want to go inside.

text.description:
The Monument to Chabuca Granda is a pair of statues in the Plazuela Chabuca Granda, right beside the Bridge of Sighs. One honours the Peruvian singer-songwriter Chabuca Granda. Next to her stands an equestrian statue of José Antonio de Lavalle y García, the man her song "José Antonio" is about. Granda spent part of her childhood on a ranch on the Bajada de los Baños, near the bridge, and in 1960 she dedicated a song to the bridge. The district later put up this tribute to her. The sculptor was Fausto Jaulis, an artist from Ayacucho, and the monument was inaugurated on 24 October 1992.

Some visitors find the monument itself underwhelming, so the surroundings matter. Try to fit the bridge, the plazuela and the figures in one frame if the angle allows, as this tells the story of the place better than a close-up of one statue. Take a wide shot first, then move in for a tighter picture of Granda or the horseman. Keep people out of the foreground if you can, or let one person stand beside a statue to show its scale. Use the gridlines to keep the bridge rails straight, and check the corners of the frame for bins and signs. If a statue looks dull on screen, try a different angle on arrival, as a few steps can change the background a lot.
text.geographic_location: In the Barranco district of Lima, in the Plazuela Chabuca Granda, next to the Puente de los Suspiros (Bridge of Sighs), near the Bajada de los Baños.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop at this spot, so head for the Bridge of Sighs area in Barranco. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to try to take in the bridge, the plazuela and the statues together. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out one statue from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Puente de los Suspiros (view from the Bajada de Baños side, looking back toward the plazuela). The small wooden-style Bridge of Sighs over the ravine, with the plazuela and its monuments framed near the approach. If they are hard to see, step onto the plazuela side for a view that includes them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: If the bridge is in your frame, use its rails as a leading line into the picture and put the statues on one of the grid thirds. Try the telephoto for a tighter portrait of Chabuca Granda or Lavalle's horse. For a different view, walk into the Plazuela Chabuca Granda and shoot toward the monument with the Puente de los Suspiros nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn gridlines on and tap the statue to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the statues do not turn into dark shapes. Portrait mode can work for a person standing beside a statue, but check that the edges look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the figures.

text.access_note: The plazuela is an outdoor public space beside the bridge, with no access restrictions.
